chapter_theme: First songs at Chidambaram (சிதம்பரம், 1 of 5): two litanies of pure praise and short pleas for vision, Siva's nectar and the five syllables open the chapter; the rest confess bondage to courtesans who sell, take money in advance, cheat and leave disease and sores behind; the praise turns on Murugan as guru to his father, on Siva and Sivakami dancing, and on Murugan with Valli in the golden hall (கனகசபை, திருச்சிற்றம்பலம்).
structure_note: Praise litanies ending பெருமாள் காண் (449, 450); short pleas for vision and grace (451, 452, 457); courtesan songs (453 to 456, 458 to 463), several ending in the diseases the women leave (456, 460, 461).

449.reading: A song of praise only, each line ending 'behold the Lord': Murugan, the poet's own guru who dwells in the golden hall, the lotus-handed light, the Lord who plays among the devotees who seek him, the pure light worshipped by Brahma, sages, gods and Arunagirinathar, the nephew of Janaki's husband, son of Sivakami, bearer of the name Muruga, the lover of the nectar-sweet hunter girl in the forest, who lives with his consorts at Puliyur.
449.nuance: அருணகிரிநாதர் appears among the worshippers, a signature of the poet inside his own praise, and எனது குருநாத makes Murugan his personal guru. Puliyur is Chidambaram. The line on golden-hued Brahma (கனகநிற வேதன் அபயமிட) is unclear.

450.reading: A second litany ending 'behold the Lord': Murugan the brother of the elephant-faced one, the guru of the Lord of chaste Sivakami, the nephew of Rama, the bearer of the victorious vel, the rider of the peacock whose wings shake the mountains, the six-faced one with pearls on his chest, the child dancing to the drum, the king of poets who threw the vel so the Suras fell, and the Lord of pure Siva-knowledge who lives at Puliyur with Valli.
450.nuance: கத்தர் குருநாத: Murugan as guru to Siva, the Lord of Sivakami, without the story told. கவிராஜப் பெருமாள் makes him king of poets, and சுத்த சிவஞானப் பெருமாள் makes him Siva-knowledge itself. வித்துருப ராமருக்கு is obscure.

451.reading: A short song: the poet asks not to wander with his mind confused by the two kinds of deed, nor to roam with his heart in the seven hells, but, through understanding that thinks on the grace of the supreme guru, to be given Murugan's vision. The praise names Murugan the Sangam poet who gave Tamil that discerns, the son of Siva with golden anklets, easy to reach for those who walk the path of compassion, the Lord in the golden hall.
451.nuance: தெரிதமிழை உதவு சங்கப் புலவோனே: Murugan is himself a poet of the Sangam who gives Tamil. கருணைநெறி புரியும் அன்பர்க்கு எளியோன்: he is easy for those who practise compassion, not only for those who worship.

452.reading: The poet asks that, praising 'Guha, supreme guru' in his heart, Siva's nectar well up on his tongue and end his hunger, that the root of the two kinds of deed, the deceits and the diseases be torn out, that he chant 'namasivaya om' with joy, and that, knowing the space with neither day nor night to be the supreme state, he be given the golden feet as Murugan comes on the peacock. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, the vel scattering Sura's forces and frightening the serpent, and Murugan who sweetly taught his father, the dancer of Kailasa, until his heart melted, the Lord in the golden hall.
452.nuance: நமசிவய ஓம்: the five syllables joined with Om. பகலும் இரவும் இலா வெளி, the space beyond day and night, names the state beyond waking and sleep. The teaching of Siva is told without naming Om (தந்தைக்கு உருக ... கொஞ்சி).

453.reading: The poet describes women with eyes like bees and carp, bow brows, cloud-dark hair, areca necks and breasts like an elephant's temples, who come down the street to cheat, call men with feigned love, embrace them and take their money; he asks that he not grieve and let his body-hut decay this way, but serve Murugan's devotees, hold the kumkum-scented feet and reach the shore. The praise is a battle in drum syllables in which the vel breaks the Suras, who had crushed the eight directions, the serpents and the hills, gives Indra back his place, and Murugan sits beside the hunter girl in the golden hall.
453.nuance: உன் அன்பருக்குச் செயல் தொண்டுபட்டு: service to the devotees is the remedy for service to the women. The line on drinking a sea (சத்திக் கடல் உண்டு) is obscure.

454.reading: The poet describes women with night-dark hair, moon faces, arrow eyes, breasts like an elephant's temples and anklets ringing, who speak like parrots and cuckoos and snatch the gold from a man's palm, and asks when his servitude to these cheats will end. The praise has conches, drums and Tamil bards sounding as the vel cuts off Sura's arms and head and sends him to Death's city, and names Kandavel who lives with the moon-faced Devayanai and the hunter girl in the golden hall.
454.nuance: அங்கை பொன் பறிக்கார பெண்கள்: women who snatch the gold from the hand. ஊழியம் செய்வது என்று போமோ: the poet names his state as servitude, the bondage that the service of the feet replaces. அண்டி மண்டையர் is obscure.

455.reading: The poet describes women with perfumed hair and breasts like white elephant tusks, who come to the bed like parrot, cuckoo and peacock, leave scars on breasts and arms and loosen their garments; he asks whether, in that infatuation, with his eyes and ears failing, he must lie with the wrongs he did before and see his body perish. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, vultures, kites and eagles crowding the field where the vel struck the deceivers, and the Lord of the devotees in the golden hall where the moon, Indra and the gods melt in praise.
455.nuance: முன்செய்த வஞ்சினங்களுடன் கிடந்து உடல் அழிவேனோ: the body is pictured dying in bed with its old deeds, the same bed as the embrace. வஞ்சினம் may mean wrongs or vows of hatred.

456.reading: The poet describes women smeared with sandal and kumkum, moon-faced and fish-eyed, who speak sweetly as though they knew a man already ('which town are you from?'), say 'come', and taste union with whoever shows gold in his hand; through them come suffering, sores with pus and worms, and colic, until the body dies and enters Death's city, and he asks for the knowledge to cross that sea and gain the feet. The praise shows gods, sages, Brahma, Vishnu, Lakshmi, Sarasvati, Arundhati and the women of every world praising the dance of Sivakami Sundari, mother of Kandavel, the vel that powders the demons' heads, and Murugan who bowed at Valli's feet in the millet field and sits in the golden hall.
456.nuance: நீர் எந்த ஊர் அறிந்தவர் போல: the courtesan's opening, feigning old acquaintance. துன்று பொன் அங்கையின் மீது கண்டவரோடு: union for whoever has gold in hand. The praise centres on Sivakami's dance, praised by the women of every world.

457.reading: The poet says he has come again and again, sprouting from seed, his body burning and his life worn away in the forest of his deceits, until he faded; he asks Murugan, pleased in heart, to come on the elephant with gods and devotees around him, scatter that forest, and appear before him with kadamba-garlanded shoulders, golden crown and lotus feet. The praise names the vel thrown at the angry demons when Vishnu, who swallowed the eight directions, fled in fear and begged for service at Murugan's feet, the lover of the hunter girl and of Devayanai, and the Lord of the dancer of the golden hall who burned the cities with a smile.
457.nuance: எந்தன் வஞ்சனைக் காடு: the forest of deceit is the poet's own, not the women's. வந்து வந்து வித்தூறி: births come one after another like seeds sprouting. The lines on the gods fleeing are hard to divide.

458.reading: The poet describes women with plaited hair, adorned necks and laughter, who grab a man's garland, madden him, bind him with coaxing, take gold until his wealth is gone and then drive him out with deceitful words, and asks whether he must wander, his desire for them satisfied and then turned bitter. The praise names the vel that crushed the demons and gave the gods back their place, Siva who burned the cities, flayed the elephant and struck off Daksha's head, and Murugan who poured the true meaning into Siva's ear, the beautiful Lord of Tiruchitrambalam.
458.nuance: பசப்பிப் பொன் தரப் பற்றிப் பொருள் மாளப் பறித்துப் பின் துரத்து: the courtesan's whole course in a line. சிவனார்தம் செவிக்குச் செம்பொருள் கற்கப் புகட்டி: Murugan teaches Siva, though Om is not named.

459.reading: The poet describes women who laugh with teeth bright as lightning, melt men and fall on them, snatch their wages in a moment, wink, wear fine cloth to show their waists, hide their breasts, give their lips' nectar, speak like cuckoos and embrace men on soft beds, and asks whether such women can be kin. The praise shows the gods hiding and crying 'Kanda, supreme', the vel slaying the demons with lions, chariots, horses and elephants while vultures and ghouls dance in blood, the son of Sivakami beside Siva who burned Kama and bears the skull, and Murugan who keeps the hunter girl in his heart and walks in Tiruchitrambalam.
459.nuance: செணத்தில் சம்பளமே பறிகாரிகள்: the women snatch a man's wages in an instant. திருச்சித்தந்தனிலே குறமானதை இருத்தி: Murugan holds Valli in his heart as the poet asks to hold the feet.

460.reading: The poet describes courtesans with parrot speech and peacock gait who cheat and snatch, take money in advance, cling until a man's debts cover him, and leave him with vomiting, colic, boils, hiccups, sorrow, cold and bile, and asks when this thief will gain a place in grace. The praise names the vel dancing while the hills burst and the guardians of the directions sing, the son of Uma, Siva's half, the wish-granting gem, the mother dear to devotees, the son who came as a merchant to deceive and win the hunter girl Valli, and the Lord of the hall where Siva dances.
460.nuance: முற்பணம் கைக்கொடும் தாரும்: 'give money in hand in advance', the courtesans' terms. In the praise Murugan comes as a merchant (செட்டியென்று எத்தி) to win Valli: the verb எத்தி, 'cheating', is the one used of the women (எத்தும் பறியர்), so by one reading the poet lets the god play the trick he condemns. Some of Uma's epithets are unclear.

461.reading: The poet describes the common women (பொதுமாதர்) who adorn and perfume themselves, laugh and call, embrace a man on the bed and take his gold, and the man who, after paying, wanders with sores that swell and eyes that fester, so that those who see him cover their eyes; he asks whether he must wander so. The praise names the vel that broke the hill and struck the demons' heads like balls into the sea while the gods rejoiced and showered flowers, the son of the Mad One who burned Kama and the cities, flayed the elephant and ruined Daksha's sacrifice, Murugan who rapped Brahma the creator on the head, and the Lord of the Chitrambalam with the hunter girl.
461.nuance: கண்டவர்க்குக் கண் புதைப்ப: the disease ends in the disgust of onlookers, the public shame that answers the private pleasure. படைத்துப் பொன்றுடைத் திட்பன் தனைக் குட்டும் படுத்தி: Brahma rapped on the head, from the story of Om, though Om itself is not named.

462.reading: The poet heaps names on courtesans: thieves who snatch wages, deceivers who intoxicate, the deaf, the blind, the stupid and the quarrelsome, who count and wrangle, ensnare with their eyes, preen and dance, and asks whether such women can be kin. The praise names the vel that broke the elephants, lions, chariots and horses of Sura when he came to ruin the sages, Brahmins and gods, the son of Siva who flayed the elephant, burned the cities with a laugh and cut off Brahma's head, and Murugan who married the daughter of the gods and the daughter of the hunters and entered the beautiful Tiruchitrambalam.
462.nuance: The plea is almost entirely a list of epithets in -இகள், each a separate insult, as in 429 and 438. Several (சிதடிகள், உதடிகள், சங்க்ய சங்கிகள்) are uncertain.

463.reading: The poet lists a woman's beauties, hair, brows, carp eyes, moon forehead, lips sweet as fruit, cuckoo voice, pearl teeth, areca neck, bamboo arms, golden necklaces and breasts like an elephant's temples, and asks whether his mind should be one that clutches at those who take even the last coin of their lovers. The praise names Vishnu who churned the sea for nectar, who shares himself with Lakshmi, who powdered the head of Lanka's king and holds the worlds in his belly, and Siva who burned the cities, and calls Murugan the son of Sankari, praised by Brahma, the Lord of the shining Ambalam.
463.nuance: The plea is almost all description, the catalogue of beauty that the closing question turns against. விண்டவர் தங்கள் தம்படியும் கவண்டிய: 'grabbing even the copper coin of those who part', but the split and subject of this line are uncertain.

links.note: Both give the courtesan's course in one sequence: the Naladiyar's woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from a man's hands and then balks like an ox; 458's coaxes, takes gold until the wealth is gone, then drives him off with deceitful words.
Both carry the courtesan song past the bed to the diseases it leaves, sores with pus and festering; 456 follows them into Death's city, 461 to the onlookers who cover their eyes.

source_issues: Song 453: corrupt character in கமுகென்பக்஡ணவம் (line 3); with ஡ண for ரீ it reads க்ரீவம் ('neck', likened to the areca palm).
